newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK industrial output seen rising in Nov.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK industrial output seen rising in Nov.

text.p: UK industrial production data due on Friday are expected to show continued steady recovery in November, with export orders largely unhampered by sterling's spectacular rise, economists said on Wednesday.
But they warned Britain's manufacturing sector was not out of the woods yet and forward-looking surveys suggested the pound's appreciation will start to bite before long.
"The CBI and purchasing managers' surveys were still reasonably optimistic in November," said Schroders economist David Philpotts.
"It wasn't until December that they started to reveal the impact sterling was having on export orders, so I expect another modest rise in manufacturing output in November."

According to a Reuter poll economists expect manufacturing output to rise 0.3 percent in November from a 0.5 percent increase in October, giving annual growth of 1.0 percent, up sharply from the previous 0.3 percent.
A rise in oil and gas extraction along with higher energy output at the start of Britain's cold snap is seen boosting the broader measure of industrial production.

"The Royal Bank of Scotland's oil and gas index points to a bounce in North Sea output after the dip in the previous month, while energy supply is also likely to have rebounded," said HSBC economist Jonathan Loynes.
Economists expect industrial production to rise 0.5 percent in November from October's unchanged rate, giving annual growth of 1.4 percent, significantly higher than October's 0.6 percent.
Sterling's meteoric 14 percent appreciation on a trade- weighted basis since August is expected to curtail foreign demand for British goods in the export-sensitive manufacturing sector.
More than half of manufacturing output is destined for overseas markets.
But the strong rebound in domestic consumption will alleviate its impact to an extent. "Sterling will weigh on the recovery rather than abort it," Philpotts said.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Ciaran Barr agreed strong domestic consumption would buoy the manufacturing sector.
"Despite the adverse effect on exports, surveys show that domestic orders continue to accelerate, led by a resurgent consumer sector," he said.

With all eyes on next week's monetary policy meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George, markets will comb the data for evidence of the strength of economic recovery in Britain.
Economists are split on the likelihood of a rate rise after the January 15 meeting, but most agree one will be necessary before the general election which must be held by May this year.
